title: Scalable Simplicity
explain: I prefer choices that are simple today and still work as the product grows, so a first success does not force a re-platform. My two standing examples: start with a JSONB column for the fast-changing parts of the data model, and run compute on serverless or container apps that scale to zero.
model:
Two standing examples:

- **Data:** keep identity, relationships and anything you filter, join or enforce on as **real columns**; put fast-changing attributes in a **JSONB** column so you avoid constant migrations while the product finds its shape. When a field proves itself: add an expression index, then promote it.

```
promote a hot JSON field:  notice it is filtered often -> expression index
   -> add column + backfill -> switch reads/writes -> remove from JSON
```

- **Compute:** serverless or container apps that **scale to zero**: pay nothing idle, capacity follows load, and the same container can later move to a cluster. Example break-even: a $40/month always-on container versus $2 per million requests is equal at 20 million requests a month; early products sit far below.

**Costs:** JSONB loses inside-document constraints, rewrites the whole value on update and makes analytics awkward ([JSON vs SQL](#/sd/f/json-vs-sql)). Scale-to-zero adds **cold starts** (keep a warm minimum instance on latency-critical paths) and fits long-lived connections poorly.

Same instinct as treating most choices as [two-way doors](#/sd/f/two-way-door): run something simple, keep the escape hatch, complicate on measured need.

details.q: A product entity's attributes change almost weekly. What schema fits scalable simplicity?
details.a: Core columns (id, owner, status, created_at) plus a JSONB column for volatile attributes, promoting fields to columns when they become query-critical. A fully normalized schema means a migration per change; an all-blob design loses ownership queries and constraints.

details.q: What does the JSONB-first approach cost?
details.a: No NOT NULL or foreign keys inside the document, filtering on nested fields needs an expression or GIN index, and updating one field typically rewrites the whole value. Those are why hot, constrained fields graduate to columns.

details.q: How do you promote a hot JSON field to a real column?
details.a: Index the JSON path first (cheap and reversible), then add the column and backfill it, switch reads and writes to the column, and only then remove the field from the JSON, so you can roll back at any earlier step.

Latency-critical endpoints with sporadic traffic, since the first request after idle pays a cold start; also long-lived connections and heavy local state. A minimum of one warm instance usually fixes the first.

details.q: When does always-on beat scale-to-zero on cost?
details.a: Past break-even. With $40/month versus $2 per million requests, that is 20 million requests/month; below it scale-to-zero is cheaper, above it always-on wins.

details.q: Is scalable simplicity just "do the cheapest thing"?
details.a: No. It means the simple choice must have a credible growth path and a cheap exit. JSONB with real key columns and a container you can move to a cluster both do; a dead-end shortcut does not.

prompts.q: Explain scalable simplicity using your data and compute examples.
points: Simple today and still works as you grow
JSONB for volatile attributes, real columns for keys
Scale-to-zero compute for pay-per-use and no capacity planning
Escape hatches: promote fields, move containers to a cluster

prompts.q: State the costs of both choices and how you mitigate each.
points: JSONB: no inner constraints, whole-value rewrites, harder analytics
Mitigate with real key columns and indexes, promote hot fields
Scale-to-zero: cold starts and poor fit for long-lived connections
Mitigate with a warm minimum instance

prompts.q: An early-stage team asks whether to start on Kubernetes with normalized schemas. Respond.
points: Ask what is measured, not hypothetical
Start simple with a clear growth path
Reversible choices are cheap; spend care on one-way doors
Re-evaluate when a concrete limit appears
